pos: n. (six times twenty; one hundred and twenty)
etymology: From six and score, Saxon scoru, twenty — from the notch cut on a tally stick at every twentieth count. Older English counted in scores, and the Authorized Version preserves the habit.
biblical_def: The word means one hundred and twenty, and its two occurrences could hardly be further apart in weight. The lesser is commercial: “And Hiram sent to the king sixscore talents of gold” (1Ki 9:14) — a sum so large it is hard to translate, paid between two kings over cedar and cities. The greater is the last verse of Jonah, and it is God's closing argument to a sulking prophet: “And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?” (Jon 4:11). A hundred and twenty thousand who cannot tell right hand from left — most take this to mean small children, though some read it of a whole city's moral ignorance. Either way the argument is the same and it is an argument from pity. God ends the book by counting. He does not appeal to Jonah's theology, which was sound; Jonah had already confessed that the LORD is “a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness” (Jon 4:2), and fled precisely because he believed it. God appeals instead to a number of children, and to the cattle, and the book simply stops there without recording whether Jonah answered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines score as twenty, a number formerly reckoned by notches or marks on a tally; hence sixscore is six times twenty, or one hundred and twenty.
webster_full: SCORE, n. [Sax. scoru, twenty.]
1. A notch or incision; hence, the number twenty, which was formerly reckoned by notches or marks on a tally.
2. A line drawn; an account or reckoning kept by notches.
Sixscore, twelvescore, and the like, are formed on this manner of reckoning.
Sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand. Jonah 4.
scriptures: Jonah 4:11
And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?
1 Kings 9:14
And Hiram sent to the king sixscore talents of gold.
Jonah 4:2

And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.
Matthew 12:41
The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.
corruption_summary: Jonah is read as a fable about tolerance, when the book ends with God counting children and the prophet's complaint being that God is too merciful.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular retelling makes Jonah a narrow bigot converted to broad-mindedness by a fish, and Nineveh a lesson in accepting other cultures. The text says something far more uncomfortable. Jonah's objection was not that the Ninevites were foreign; it was that they were wicked and that God would forgive them if they repented — and they did, and He did. Jonah 4:2 is a confession of orthodox theology offered as a grievance. The prophet knew the doctrine of God's mercy perfectly and hated it when it was aimed away from his own people. That is a sin available to the most conservative heart, and the book was written for it.

The historical-critical tradition treats the whole account as parable, and Matthew 12:41 is the reason the dictionary does not: the Lord Jesus cites the men of Nineveh as men who will rise in judgment, and stakes His own sign on Jonah's three days. A fictional Nineveh cannot rise in judgment against anybody. And the closing number matters for the same reason: sixscore thousand is a count, not a flourish. God ends His book by telling a prophet how many small children live in a city he wanted burned, which is the strongest statement in the Old Testament that divine mercy is not sentimental and is not abstract. It is numbered.
roots_summary: Hebrew me'ah 'esrim ribbo, a hundred and twenty thousand; kikkar (H3603), a talent; Saxon scoru, twenty.
roots_lines: Hebrew shetteym 'esreh ribbo — twelve myriads, a hundred and twenty thousand; Jonah 4:11.
Hebrew kikkar zahab (H3603, H2091) — a talent of gold, a circular weight; 1 Kings 9:14, sixscore of them.
Hebrew chus (H2347) — to pity, to spare; the verb God uses of Nineveh and Jonah used of his gourd.
Hebrew chanun werachum (H2587, H7349) — gracious and merciful; Jonah 4:2, quoting Exodus 34:6 as a complaint.
Saxon scoru — twenty, from a notch on a tally; Webster's root behind every -score in the English Bible.
usage: “Sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left” — God's closing argument is a count of children.
“I knew that thou art a gracious God” — sound doctrine, offered as a grievance.
“Sixscore talents of gold” — the same number, doing much smaller work.

pos: n. (a dish or portion of food sent to a person at table)
etymology: Old French mes, a dish sent to table, from Latin missus, sent, from mittere, to send. A mess is literally a sending — a portion dispatched from the host's table to a guest, which is why it was an act of honour.
biblical_def: A mess in the Authorized Version is a portion of food sent from the host's own table, and the sending is an act of favour whose size carries a message. Joseph, still unrecognized by his brothers, hosts them in Egypt: “And he took and sent messes unto them from before him: but Benjamin's mess was five times so much as any of theirs. And they drank, and were merry with him” (Gen 43:34). Joseph is testing. He heaps the plate of the youngest — the other son of Rachel, the new favourite — to see whether these men will do to Benjamin what they once did to him. They eat and are merry, and the envy does not surface, and Joseph has his answer. The second occurrence is a mess sent with murderous intent: “And David said to Uriah, Go down to thy house, and wash thy feet. And Uriah departed out of the king's house, and there followed him a mess of meat from the king” (2Sa 11:8). The king's generous portion follows a soldier home, and its whole purpose is to get him to sleep with his wife so an adultery can be covered. The same courtesy, in one case testing hearts and in the other baiting a trap.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mess as a dish or a quantity of food prepared or set on a table at one time; and a set of four persons who eat together, as in a ship or regiment.
webster_full: MESS, n. [Fr. mets, a dish of meat; from L. missus, sent, from mitto, to send.]
1. A dish or a quantity of food prepared or set on a table at one time; as a mess of pottage.
Benjamin's mess was five times so much as any of theirs. Gen. 43.
2. A number of persons who eat together; among seamen and soldiers, a set of four.
3. A medley; a mixed mass. A mess of meat was a portion sent from the host's table as a mark of honor.
scriptures: Genesis 43:34
And he took and sent messes unto them from before him: but Benjamin's mess was five times so much as any of theirs. And they drank, and were merry with him.
2 Samuel 11:8
And David said to Uriah, Go down to thy house, and wash thy feet. And Uriah departed out of the king's house, and there followed him a mess of meat from the king.
Genesis 37:4
And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.
Genesis 50:20
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that hospitality is never morally neutral — it may test a heart or bait a trap.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The English word has drifted to mean disorder or a soldiers' table, and nothing is being contested. What the two texts hold is a doctrine about ordinary kindness that the church seldom teaches: a favour done is an act with a moral direction, and the same act may serve opposite ends. Joseph's heaped plate for Benjamin repeats, deliberately, the exact circumstance that had destroyed the family — the father's favourite, visibly preferred — and Joseph does it to find out whether his brothers are different men now. Genesis 37:4 records what the old favouritism produced; Genesis 43:34 records that this time they ate and were merry.

The principle to recover is discernment about generosity, both given and received. David's mess of meat to Uriah was lavish, royal, and entirely corrupt in purpose, and Uriah's refusal to go down to his house is one of the quiet heroisms of the Old Testament — a Hittite mercenary keeping faith with the ark and the army while the king of Israel worked to compromise him. Christians who receive a sudden and generous portion from a powerful hand do well to ask what it is for. And Genesis 50:20 supplies the end of Joseph's story: his brothers thought evil against him, but God meant it unto good.
roots_summary: Hebrew mas'eth (H4864), a portion lifted and sent; mishneh, a double portion; Latin missus, sent, from mittere.
roots_lines: Hebrew mas'oth (H4864) — portions lifted up and carried; Genesis 43:34, the messes sent from Joseph's table.
Hebrew chamesh yadoth — five hands, five times; the size of Benjamin's portion and the whole point of the test.
Hebrew mas'ath hammelek — the king's portion; 2 Samuel 11:8, the gift that followed Uriah home.
Latin missus, from mittere — sent; Webster's root, a dish dispatched from the host.
Hebrew shalach (H7971) — to send; the same idea underlying the whole custom of sending portions, as at Purim in Esther 9:19.
usage: “Benjamin's mess was five times so much” — a test disguised as a favour.
“There followed him a mess of meat from the king” — a favour disguising a trap.
“They drank, and were merry with him” — and the envy did not come.

pos: n. (a measure of land; originally as much as a yoke of oxen could plough in a day)
etymology: Saxon aecer, a field, cognate with Latin ager and Greek agros, a field. The measure was not fixed by survey but by labour — what one team could turn in a day.
biblical_def: The Hebrew has no acre; the Authorized Version supplies an English farmer's word for a Hebrew measure taken from the plough, and both occurrences make theological use of the size of a field. The first gives the dimensions of a victory: “And that first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armourbearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were an half acre of land, which a yoke of oxen might plow” (1Sa 14:14). Two men, twenty enemies, half an acre — the narrator is at pains to record how small the ground was, because the point of the chapter is that “there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few”. The second gives the dimensions of a judgment: “Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah” (Isa 5:10). Ten acres of vines producing a single bath — perhaps eight gallons — and a homer of seed returning a tenth of itself. This is the curse pronounced on the men who join house to house and field to field until there is no place left. They gathered acres, and God emptied them. Both verses measure land to make a point about who actually gives the increase.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acre as a quantity of land containing 160 square rods or perches, and notes that in its primitive sense it signified an open field, and among our ancestors, as much land as a yoke of oxen could plow in a day.
webster_full: A'CRE, n. a'ker. [Sax. aecer, aecera, a field; L. ager; Gr. agros.]
1. In its primitive sense, an open field.
2. In Great Britain, a quantity of land, containing 160 square rods or perches, or 4840 square yards.
This was as much land as a yoke of oxen could plow in a day, whence the Latin jugerum.
Half an acre of land, which a yoke of oxen might plow. 1 Sam. 14.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 14:14
And that first slaughter, which Jonathan and his armourbearer made, was about twenty men, within as it were an half acre of land, which a yoke of oxen might plow.
Isaiah 5:10
Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah.
Isaiah 5:8
Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
1 Samuel 14:6

And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 5:8 is either dismissed as an ancient land regulation or pressed into a modern redistribution programme; the prophet is doing neither.
corruption_paragraphs: The woe on those who join house to house and lay field to field is often read as a general condemnation of wealth or private ownership, and it is neither. Israel's land was distributed by tribe and family under a law that included jubilee, so that no household could be permanently dispossessed of its inheritance. The sin Isaiah names is the systematic accumulation that emptied the countryside till there be no place — men made landless in a covenant order designed to prevent exactly that. The dictionary holds private property as a creation ordinance protected by the eighth commandment; what Isaiah condemns is not ownership but the engrossing of a nation's inheritance into a few hands.

The judgment is worth noting because it is not confiscation. God does not redistribute the acres; He makes them barren. Ten acres yield a bath, and a homer of seed returns an ephah, so the men who gathered the fields keep them and gain nothing. That is a sharper answer than any policy, and it is the recurring biblical pattern: the increase is God's to give or withhold, and a man may own a great deal of ground and harvest nothing from it. Jonathan's half acre points the same way from the other side — a very small field, two men, and a victory nobody could attribute to resources.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsemed (H6776), a yoke or pair, hence the land a yoke ploughs; bath (H1324), a liquid measure; homer (H2563) and ephah (H374), dry measures; Saxon aecer, a field.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsemed sadeh (H6776) — a yoke of field, the ground a pair of oxen ploughs; 1 Samuel 14:14 and Isaiah 5:10.
Hebrew bath (H1324) — the liquid measure, roughly an ephah in volume; the whole yield of ten acres under the curse.
Hebrew homer (H2563) — a large dry measure, ten ephahs; so the seed returned a tenth of itself.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance; the tribal land-grant Isaiah 5:8 is defending.
Saxon aecer, Latin ager, Greek agros — a field; Webster's root, a measure defined by a day's ploughing.
usage: “Within as it were an half acre of land” — the narrator measures the ground to make the point.
“Ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath” — they keep the fields and get nothing.
“There is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” — Jonathan's theology before the climb.

pos: n. (a set piece of work, especially one imposed by another; a stint required within a set time)
etymology: Old French tasque, from Latin taxare, to rate or appraise — the same root as tax. A task is an assessed quantity of labour, levied as a tax is levied, and the Authorized Version uses it only of slavery.
biblical_def: Both occurrences stand in Exodus 5, in the week Pharaoh doubled the pressure because Moses had asked for a feast in the wilderness. The officers of Israel “did see that they were in evil case, after it was said, Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task” (Exo 5:19). The straw was withdrawn and the quota was not: “Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks” (Exo 5:18). That is the exact anatomy of oppression — the demand held constant while the means are removed — and Scripture records it in administrative detail rather than in generalities. The chapter before had already summarized the system: “And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour” (Exo 1:14). The word task in the Bible therefore always has a taskmaster standing over it, and its only use is Egypt. Against it the New Testament sets a different summons from a different Master: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines task as business imposed by another, often a definite quantity or amount of labor; work to be done within a given time; and by extension, burdensome employment.
webster_full: TASK, n. [Fr. tache; Arm. tasq; from the root of tax.]
1. Business imposed by another, often a definite quantity or amount of labor.
Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task. Ex. 5.
2. Business; employment; undertaking; that which duty or necessity imposes.
3. Burdensome employment; toil; labor imposed and often oppressive. To take to task, to reprove; to reprimand.
scriptures: Exodus 5:19
And the officers of the children of Israel did see that they were in evil case, after it was said, Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task.
Exodus 5:18
Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks.
Exodus 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
Matthew 11:28
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Religion of every age reproduces Pharaoh's arrangement — the quota kept and the straw withdrawn — and calls it discipleship.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 5:18 is the permanent description of works-religion: there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks. The standard remains absolute; the resources are removed; and the failure is charged to the worker. Every system that requires a man to justify himself runs on that arrangement, whether it is Rome's ladder of merit, a legalistic congregation's unwritten quota of activity, or the private tyranny of a conscience that will not accept a finished work. Moses did not negotiate the quota down. God broke the system and brought the people out.

There is a further point that cuts closer to home. The word task in Scripture is always Egyptian, and the New Testament's word for Christian work is not this one. Believers labour, strive, run, and fight — the vocabulary is strenuous — but the labour proceeds from rest rather than toward it. Matthew 11:28 offers rest first and then hands out a yoke, which is exactly the reverse of Pharaoh's order. A ministry that leaves its people feeling watched, measured, and behind has reinvented Exodus 5 with better vocabulary, and the tell is always the same: the demand rises and no one ever delivers the straw.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar yom beyomo, the matter of a day in its day; oved perek (H5656, H6531), service with rigour; Latin taxare, to rate or assess.
roots_lines: Hebrew debar yom beyomo — the thing of a day in its day; Exodus 5:19, the daily task as a fixed levy.
Hebrew perek (H6531) — harshness, rigour, breaking; Exodus 1:14, the manner of the service.
Hebrew nogesim (H5065) — taskmasters, drivers, exactors; the men set over the quota.
Hebrew tokhen halebenim — the measure, the tale of the bricks; Exodus 5:18, the count that would not move.
Latin taxare — to rate, appraise; Webster's root, shared with tax: a task is labour levied.
usage: “No straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks” — the anatomy of every works-religion.
“All their service… was with rigour” — the system summarized in one word.
“Come unto me… and I will give you rest” — rest first, then the yoke.

pos: n. (the sense or purport of a thing; the general drift; the substance as distinct from the exact words)
etymology: Latin tenor, a holding on, a continuous course, from tenere, to hold. The tenor of a discourse is what it holds throughout — its sustained sense, not a single phrase lifted out.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version uses tenor, and both times it means the substance or purport of words. Joseph's brothers, defending themselves to Jacob, say: “The man asked us straitly of our state, and of our kindred, saying, Is your father yet alive? have ye another brother? and we told him according to the tenor of these words” (Gen 43:7). They answered according to the drift of what was asked, not by reciting a script. The second occurrence is far weightier, since it concerns the covenant document itself: “And the LORD said unto Moses, Write thou these words: for after the tenor of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel” (Exo 34:27). The covenant is made after the tenor of the words — according to their sustained sense, the whole drift of what was spoken on the mount — and Moses is commanded to write them. Both halves matter. The covenant is verbal and written, not a vague disposition; and it is according to the tenor, which forbids the lawyer's trick of isolating a clause against the whole. Scripture is to be read the way a covenant is read: every word binding, and no word against the drift of the rest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tenor as continued run or currency; a general course or drift; purport; substance; and the general or prevailing course or manner.
webster_full: TEN'OR, n. [L. tenor, from teneo, to hold.]
1. Continued run or currency; whole course or strain.
Along the tenor of his life.
2. Stamp; character; nature.
3. Sense contained; purport; substance; general course or drift. Warrants of a like tenor. After the tenor of these words I have made a covenant. Ex. 34.
scriptures: Exodus 34:27
And the LORD said unto Moses, Write thou these words: for after the tenor of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel.
Genesis 43:7

And they said, The man asked us straitly of our state, and of our kindred, saying, Is your father yet alive? have ye another brother? and we told him according to the tenor of these words: could we certainly know that he would say, Bring your brother down?
Deuteronomy 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Both errors are errors about tenor: the proof-texter isolates a clause from the drift, and the critic dissolves the drift and keeps no clause at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 34:27 joins two things the modern mind keeps trying to separate: write thou these words, and after the tenor of these words. The covenant is verbal — particular words, written down, not to be added to or diminished (Deu 4:2) — and it is also a sustained sense that runs through the whole. The proof-texter honours the first and violates the second, lifting a clause out of its drift to make it say what the passage as a whole denies; this is how nearly every heresy is built, and how Satan quoted Psalm 91 in the wilderness. The Reformed rule of interpreting Scripture by Scripture exists precisely to keep tenor and text together.

The liberal error runs the other way and is now the more common. Once the drift is granted to be a general spirit of love or liberation, the particular words become expendable, and the text is read for its trajectory rather than its content. That is not reading according to tenor; it is replacing the tenor with one of our own and then attributing it to God. 2 Timothy 3:16 says all scripture is God-breathed — which makes the words themselves the deposit, and their sustained sense the way they are to be read. Neither the clause without the drift nor the drift without the clause is the covenant Moses was told to write.
roots_summary: Hebrew al pi (H6310), according to the mouth of; dibre (H1697), words, matters; Latin tenor, from tenere, to hold.
roots_lines: Hebrew al pi haddebarim ha'elleh (H6310, H1697) — according to the mouth of these words; Exodus 34:27, rendered after the tenor.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, and also a matter or thing; the Hebrew refuses to separate the saying from the substance.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; a cut bond, made here according to written words.
Hebrew lo tosiphu… welo tigre'u (H3254, H1639) — ye shall not add, neither diminish; Deuteronomy 4:2.
Latin tenor, from tenere — a holding on, an unbroken course; Webster's root.
usage: “After the tenor of these words I have made a covenant” — written words, and their sustained sense.
“We told him according to the tenor of these words” — the drift, faithfully given.
“Ye shall not add… neither shall ye diminish” — the guard on both ends.

pos: n. (the craw or first stomach of a bird); v.t. (to cut off the top; to pluck)
etymology: Saxon crop, the top or head of a plant, and also the craw of a fowl. Both senses survive in the Authorized Version: the bird's craw in Leviticus, and the verb to crop off a tender twig in Ezekiel.
biblical_def: The noun belongs to the poor man's offering. When a worshipper could not afford a lamb he brought turtledoves or young pigeons, and the priest “shall pluck away his crop with his feathers, and cast it beside the altar on the east part, by the place of the ashes” (Lev 1:16) — the crop being the bird's craw, the pouch that holds what it has eaten off the ground. Even in the cheapest sacrifice in the law, the refuse is removed before the offering ascends. God does not become less particular as the offering becomes less costly; the poor man's dove is prepared with the same care as the bullock. The verb appears in Ezekiel's parable of the cedar, and it is Messianic: “I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent” (Eze 17:22). God Himself does the cropping. A tender shoot is taken from the top of a felled royal house and planted on a high mountain, and it becomes a great tree sheltering every fowl — the Davidic line cut down to a stump and raised again in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crop as the first stomach of a fowl, the craw; the top or highest part of a plant; and as a verb, to cut off the ends, to pluck, to mow or reap.
webster_full: CROP, n. [Sax. crop, the top or head of a plant, also the craw of a fowl.]
1. The first stomach of a fowl; the craw.
He shall pluck away his crop with his feathers. Lev. 1.
2. The top or highest part of a plant; the end or shoot.
3. That which is gathered; the corn or fruits of the earth collected. CROP, v.t. To cut off the ends of any thing; to pluck; to mow or reap.
scriptures: Leviticus 1:16
And he shall pluck away his crop with his feathers, and cast it beside the altar on the east part, by the place of the ashes:
Ezekiel 17:22

Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent:
Leviticus 1:14
And if the burnt sacrifice for his offering to the LORD be of fowls, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves, or of young pigeons.
Isaiah 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, he shall not desire him.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is as exact about the poor man's offering as about the rich man's.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is contesting the word. What Leviticus 1:16 holds is a principle the church loses in both directions. The bird offering existed because some worshippers could not afford a lamb; the law made a way for the poor man to come. And yet the law does not become casual because the offering is cheap — the crop and the feathers are removed, the ashes have a place, the east side is specified. Mercy toward the poor and exactness in worship are not in competition. A congregation that thinks care about the ordinances is a luxury of the comfortable has misread the cheapest sacrifice in the book.

The principle to recover, then, is the regulative instinct applied evenly: God says how He will be approached, and He says it as carefully to the man with two pigeons as to the man with a bullock. Ezekiel 17:22 carries the same word into prophecy, and there the tenderness is the point — a tender one cropped from the top of a ruined house and planted by God on a high mountain. Isaiah saw the same shoot: he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground. The cropping looks like loss, and it is how the kingdom came.
roots_summary: Hebrew mur'ah (H4760), the crop or craw of a bird; qataph (H6998), to pluck off; Saxon crop, the top of a plant or the craw of a fowl.
roots_lines: Hebrew mur'ah (H4760) — the crop, craw of a bird; Leviticus 1:16, and found nowhere else in Scripture.
Hebrew notsah (H5133) — the feathers or plumage cast aside with it.
Hebrew eqtoph (H6998) — I will crop off, pluck; Ezekiel 17:22, with God as the one plucking.
Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft; the young shoot of Ezekiel 17:22 and the tender plant of Isaiah 53:2.
Saxon crop — the top of a plant, the craw of a fowl; Webster's root, holding both senses at once.
usage: “Pluck away his crop with his feathers” — the poor man's offering, prepared with full care.
“I will crop off… a tender one” — and God is the one doing the cropping.
“As a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground” — the same shoot, seen by Isaiah.

pos: n. (a regular allowance of food; the daily provision assigned to a person)
etymology: Greek diaita, a way of living, from which Latin diaeta and French diete. The older sense is not what one eats to lose weight but the settled provision by which one lives.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it closes the book of Jeremiah — a book that began with a nation under sentence and ends with a captive king at a foreign table. Jehoiachin, carried to Babylon as a youth and imprisoned thirty-seven years, is released by Evil-merodach: “And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life” (Jer 52:34). The parallel account adds that his prison garments were changed and that he ate bread continually before the king. Note the words continual, every day, all the days of his life — Jeremiah piles them up. It is the last note of a book of judgment, and it is a note of preservation: the line of David is not extinct, it is fed at a pagan king's table, and Matthew's genealogy will run straight through this man to Christ. Scripture repeatedly ends its darkest sections with a daily provision rather than a dramatic rescue — the same pattern as manna, as the widow's barrel, and as the petition the Lord taught: give us this day our daily bread.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diet as food or victuals; a regular course of eating and drinking prescribed; and an allowance of provision.
webster_full: DI'ET, n. [Gr. diaita, manner of living; L. diaeta.]
1. Food or victuals.
2. Food prescribed by a physician, with respect to quantity and quality.
3. Allowance of provision. For his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon. Jer. 52.
DI'ET, v.t. To feed; to board; to furnish provisions for.
scriptures: Jeremiah 52:34
And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
Jeremiah 52:33
And changed his prison garments: and he did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life.
2 Kings 25:30
And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.
Matthew 6:11
Give us this day our daily bread.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's ordinary preservation of His promises looks like a daily ration, not a rescue.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The English word has narrowed to mean a regimen of eating, and nothing doctrinal is at stake in the drift. What is at stake is how the last paragraph of Jeremiah is read. A book that has spent fifty-two chapters on the destruction of Jerusalem ends with a released prisoner and a food allowance, and many readers pass over it as an administrative footnote. It is nothing of the sort. The covenant with David hung by this thread, and the thread is described as a continual diet… every day a portion… all the days of his life.

The principle to recover is patience with ordinary provision. God's way of keeping His promises is very often a daily ration at somebody else's table rather than a deliverance anyone would write a song about. Israel in the wilderness got manna each morning and no more; the widow of Zarephath got a barrel that did not empty rather than a granary; and the Lord taught His disciples to ask for bread this day. A church that can only see God at work in the spectacular will read Jeremiah 52 as an anticlimax, when it is in fact the hinge on which the genealogy of Christ turns.
roots_summary: Hebrew aruchah (H737), an allowance, a regular meal; debar yom beyomo, the portion of a day in its day; Greek diaita, manner of living.
roots_lines: Hebrew aruchah (H737) — an allowance, a settled ration; Jeremiah 52:34 and 2 Kings 25:30.
Hebrew aruchath tamid (H8548) — a continual allowance; tamid is the same word used of the continual burnt offering.
Hebrew debar yom beyomo — the matter of a day in its day; the manna formula of Exodus 16:4.
Greek epiousion (G1967) — daily, for the coming day; Matthew 6:11, the bread asked for one day at a time.
Greek diaita — a way of living; Webster's root, before the English narrowed it to regimen.
usage: “A continual diet… every day a portion… all the days of his life” — Jeremiah piles the words up.
“He did continually eat bread before him” — the Davidic line, fed at a pagan table.
“Give us this day our daily bread” — the same arrangement, taught as a prayer.

pos: n. pl. (deeds; acts of note; in Daniel, decisive action taken with effect)
etymology: Old French exploit, from Latin explicitum, a thing unfolded or accomplished, from explicare, to unfold. An exploit is a thing carried out to its end.
biblical_def: Both occurrences stand in the eleventh chapter of Daniel, four verses apart, and they are set deliberately against each other. The first belongs to the persecutor: “Then shall he return into his land with great riches; and his heart shall be against the holy covenant; and he shall do exploits, and return to his own land” (Dan 11:28). The second belongs to those he persecutes: “And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits” (Dan 11:32). The same verb, two armies. And the difference is stated exactly: the tyrant does exploits out of great riches and a heart against the covenant; the faithful do exploits because they know their God. Daniel then tells us what the exploits of the second sort actually look like, and it is not what the word suggests to modern ears: “they that understand among the people shall instruct many: yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days” (Dan 11:33). Teaching, and then dying. The exploits of those who know God are catechesis and martyrdom, and the chapter counts both as strength.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exploit as a deed or act; more especially, a heroic act; a deed of renown; a great or noble achievement.
webster_full: EXPLOIT', n. [Fr. exploit; L. explicitum, from explico, to unfold.]
1. A deed or act; more especially, a heroic act; a deed of renown; a great or noble achievement.
The people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits. Dan. 11.
2. In a general sense, any performance or accomplishment.
EXPLOIT', v.t. To achieve; to accomplish. The root sense is a thing unfolded and carried through.
scriptures: Daniel 11:32
And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits.
Daniel 11:28
Then shall he return into his land with great riches; and his heart shall be against the holy covenant; and he shall do exploits, and return to his own land.
Daniel 11:33
And they that understand among the people shall instruct many: yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days.
Daniel 3:17
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
corruption_summary: “Do exploits” has become a slogan for triumphalist ministry, when Daniel's own next verse defines it as teaching and dying.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 11:32 is quoted constantly as a promise of visible triumph — conferences, movements, and mission slogans built on the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits. The verse is true and the promise is real; the trouble is that readers stop before verse 33, which tells us what the exploits are: they that understand among the people shall instruct many: yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days. Instructing many, and falling. Daniel's exploits are a catechism class and a martyrdom, sustained over many days with no deliverance in sight. Any use of this verse that promises something more impressive than that has improved on the prophet.

The chapter also names the method of the other side, and it is not force: such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries. Persecution takes the faithful by the sword and takes the compromisers by compliment. That is the older and more effective instrument, and it is at work in every age where a church can gain standing by softening a doctrine. The counter is knowledge of God — not zeal, not strategy, but knowing Him, which is why Daniel's three friends could say our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, and then add but if not. Men who know God are strong because their obedience does not depend on the outcome.
roots_summary: Hebrew asah (H6213), to do, to act with effect; yada (H3045), to know; chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to prevail; Latin explicare, to unfold.
roots_lines: Hebrew we'asah (H6213) — and he shall do; the Hebrew of Daniel 11:28 and 11:32 has simply act, and the Authorized Version supplies exploits.
Hebrew yode'e elohaw (H3045) — the knowers of their God; a participle, not a title — those who are knowing Him.
Hebrew yachaziqu (H2388) — they shall be strong, take firm hold; the same root as Hezekiah's name.
Hebrew maskile am (H7919) — the wise, the instructors among the people; Daniel 11:33, those who teach and fall.
Latin explicare, explicitum — to unfold, a thing carried through; Webster's root.
usage: “The people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits” — and verse 33 says what they are.
“Shall he corrupt by flatteries” — the sword takes the faithful; the compliment takes the rest.
“Instruct many: yet they shall fall” — catechesis and martyrdom, counted as strength.

pos: a. (attentive; intent; heedful — an archaic form of attentive)
etymology: Latin attentus, from attendere, to stretch toward, from ad- and tendere. The picture is of a man leaning in — the ear stretched toward the speaker.
biblical_def: This archaic form of attentive occurs twice, and the two verses are a petition and its answer, separated by a chapter. At the dedication of the temple Solomon prays: “Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and let thine ears be attent unto the prayer that is made in this place” (2Ch 6:40). Then the LORD appears to him by night and gives the answer back almost word for word: “Now mine eyes shall be open, and mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place” (2Ch 7:15). The repetition is the point. God takes the king's own words and returns them as a promise, and the only change is from petition to declaration — let thine ears be becomes mine ears shall be. Solomon had already confessed that no house could contain Him — “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built?” (2Ch 6:18) — so the promise is not that God is localized but that He has appointed a place where He undertakes to listen. And the condition attached is the famous one immediately before it: if my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines attent as attentive; intent; and marks it as obsolete in ordinary use, surviving chiefly in the Scripture phrase, let thine ears be attent.
webster_full: ATTENT', a. [L. attentus.]
Attentive; intent.
Let thine ears be attent to the prayer that is made in this place. 2 Chron. 6.
The word is now obsolete in common discourse, being superseded by attentive.
From attendo, ad and tendo, to stretch toward; the ear stretched toward the speaker.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 6:40
Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and let thine ears be attent unto the prayer that is made in this place.
2 Chronicles 7:15
Now mine eyes shall be open, and mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place.
2 Chronicles 7:14

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
2 Chronicles 6:18
But will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth? behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built!
corruption_summary: 2 Chronicles 7:14 has been lifted out of this temple context and applied to modern nations as a covenant promise God never made to them.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse standing between these two occurrences — if my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves — is probably the most misapplied text in American religious life, printed on banners and quoted at rallies as a national promise. Its address is specific: it is spoken to Solomon about the temple just dedicated, to a people in covenant, whose land was given them by oath, and it concerns that house and that land. No modern nation stands in Israel's covenantal place. The dictionary does not on that account dismiss the verse; the God who said it has not changed, and humility, prayer, seeking His face and turning from wickedness are always the way sinners approach Him. But a promise made to a covenant people about a particular house is not a policy lever, and using it as one has taught a generation to expect national revival as a transaction.

The second corruption is more devotional and more common: reading God's attentiveness as unconditional and generic, as though He were obliged to hear anyone on any terms. 2 Chronicles 6:18 blocks that from the other side by confessing the transcendence — the heaven of heavens cannot contain Him, and it is pure condescension that He appoints any place at all. Under the new covenant the appointed place is not a building but a Person; access is through the one Mediator, and the ear stretched toward us was purchased. That is a better promise than Solomon had, and it is not a looser one.
roots_summary: Hebrew qashab (H7183), attentive, giving ear; oznayim qashuboth, ears attent; Latin attendere, to stretch toward.
roots_lines: Hebrew qashshuboth (H7183) — attentive, open to hear; 2 Chronicles 6:40 and 7:15, of the ears of God.
Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to prick up the ear, to incline and listen; the root, used of a man leaning toward a sound.
Hebrew kanaph … yikkane'u (H3665) — shall humble themselves, be brought low; 2 Chronicles 7:14.
Hebrew shemey hashamayim — the heaven of heavens; 2 Chronicles 6:18, which cannot contain Him.
Latin attentus, from ad- and tendere — stretched toward; Webster's root, now surviving only as attentive.
usage: “Let thine ears be attent” — Solomon's petition at the dedication.
“Mine ears attent unto the prayer that is made in this place” — the same words, returned as promise.
“The heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” — said by the man building Him a house.

pos: n. (dulness of sight or of light; obscurity; want of clearness)
etymology: From dim, Saxon dim, dark, obscure. In Isaiah the word names a gloom that is moral and national before it is optical — the darkness a people walk in when they have turned from the law and the testimony.
biblical_def: Isaiah has the word twice, in consecutive chapters, and the second overturns the first. The end of chapter eight describes what a nation finds when it consults the dead instead of the living God: “And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness” (Isa 8:22). Dimness of anguish — the gloom of a people whose sight has failed because their source of light was abandoned. Then chapter nine opens with a nevertheless: “Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations” (Isa 9:1). Those two regions were the first to be carried away by Assyria — the darkest corner of the land — and they are named because that is exactly where the light will rise: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa 9:2). Matthew quotes it of Christ beginning His ministry in Capernaum (Mat 4:16). The dimness is dispelled at the precise point where it was deepest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dimness as dulness of sight; obscurity of vision; want of clearness or lustre; and figuratively, dulness of apprehension.
webster_full: DIM'NESS, n.
1. Dulness of sight; obscurity of vision from a fault in the organs or from distance.
2. Dulness of apprehension; stupidity.
The dimness of my intellectual eye.
3. Want of clearness or lustre. The dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation. Is. 9. From dim, Sax. dim, dark, obscure.
scriptures: Isaiah 8:22
And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness.
Isaiah 9:1

Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations.
Isaiah 9:2
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.
Matthew 4:16
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 8 traces the dimness to consulting the dead rather than the law and the testimony — a practice the age has revived under new names.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter that ends in dimness of anguish begins with a specific charge: a people told to seek unto those that have familiar spirits, and answered with to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. The dimness is diagnosed, not merely lamented. Its cause is a nation seeking guidance from anywhere except the written word of God. Every generation reopens that door under fresh branding — mediums and horoscopes plainly, but also the softer forms in which a Christian looks for direction to impressions, signs, and inner voices held above the Scripture rather than tested by it. The prophet's remedy is not more intense seeking; it is a book.

Isaiah 9:1 then does something no purely moral diagnosis could do. It names the two tribes that had suffered first and worst under Assyria, the darkest and most despised region of the land, and promises that the light will rise there. Matthew 4:16 records the fulfilment when Christ leaves Nazareth and settles in Capernaum, by the way of the sea, in Galilee of the nations. That is the Reformed doctrine of grace in geography: God does not begin where the light is already best. He begins in the dimness, which is why no man's condition is an argument against his being saved.
roots_summary: Hebrew mu'aph (H4155), gloom, dimness; tsuqah (H6695), anguish, straitness; chashekah (H2825), darkness; Saxon dim, obscure.
roots_lines: Hebrew mu'aph (H4155) — gloom, dimness; Isaiah 8:22 and 9:1, and found almost nowhere else.
Hebrew tsuqah (H6695) — anguish, distress, narrowness; the dimness of anguish is a gloom that also crowds.
Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757) — the shadow of death; Isaiah 9:2, the same word as in Psalm 23:4.
Hebrew Galil haggoyim (H1551, H1471) — Galilee of the nations; the despised northern region where the light rose.
Saxon dim — dark, obscure; Webster's root.
usage: “Trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish” — a gloom that crowds as well as blinds.
“Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such” — the turn of the whole prophecy.
“The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” — and it rose where it was darkest.
